title: A Simple Tweak for Tracking Moments of Genuine Connection in Band
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. profiles Clint Roberts, a band director at Oak Canyon Junior High School in Lindon, Utah, who adapted Stuart's "moments of genuine connection" (MGC) tracking system to the unique demands of a band classroom. Roberts built a seating chart from scanned student photos, then used a red dry-erase marker for daily attendance and blue and green dot markers to track MGCs and public-speaking opportunities (conducting the band) respectively. Stuart argues the tool will pay off because consistent tracking reveals a teacher's "connection blindspots," normalizes public speaking for students who fear it most, and builds credibility over time. He closes by praising Roberts for translating a strategy from outside his own discipline into a workable band-room system, framing it as a model of professional flexibility.
points: Roberts adapted the MGC clipboard-tracking system to band class using color-coded dots: blue for genuine-connection moments, green for public-speaking (conducting) opportunities.
Consistent MGC tracking surfaces a teacher's "connection blindspots" — the students who quietly go missed week after week.
Making conducting a normal, expected activity helps desensitize students to the fear of public speaking, one of the scariest parts of school for many.
The strategy demonstrates that good classroom tools transfer across disciplines — an ELA/history-rooted idea reshaped successfully for a band classroom.
quotes: I wanted to run with your concept of "Moments of Genuine Connection" tracking sheet but in context for band. At the beginning of the year I was cutting out student photos and scanning them to create a seating chart. It took forever but was worth it to put students' faces and names together.

After printing the chart I put it into a clear sheet in my attendance binder that stays on my conductors music stand. I'm going to take roll with a red dry erase marker and erase it each day when it goes in the computer. I'll be using Blue and Green to mark which students have had certain opportunities in class.

Blue dots will be students with whom I've had a Moment of Genuine Connection. Green dots will be students who have had an opportunity to conduct the band either in warm-ups or a song (public speaking).
As he practices moments of genuine connection with every student on his roster, he'll get better and he'll start to see the profound effects of "the dumbest intervention ever.

He'll begin to detect where his connection blindspots are — who are the students that he has the easiest time missing, week after week? Why? These questions will deepen him in his understanding of himself.

He'll create a classroom where public speaking — in this case, conducting the band — is normal rather than weird. This normalization of what for many students is the scariest thing about school will make Clint's classroom an even more special place in the memories of his students.
Clint is going to succeed because he thought up this strategy while listening to a guy who's only ever taught 6-12 grade English language arts and history.
